script.title: Why the Killer Mould Came From Downstairs

lines: A scientist smeared germs on dishes, left them out, and went on holiday.
This was Alexander Fleming, in London, in 1928.
Fleming was not a tidy researcher.
He left the dishes on a bench in a corner of his laboratory.
In September 1928, Fleming came back.
One dish was spoiled by a mould.
Around the mould, the germs had been destroyed.
Germs farther away were normal.
Fleming remarked that it was funny.
Fleming grew the mould.
Its juice killed germs that cause pneumonia.
In 1929, Fleming named the substance penicillin.
But Fleming could not make penicillin in large amounts.
Chemists failed to purify it.
Penicillin lay largely forgotten.
In 1936, Fleming spoke of its value in London.
No one believed him.
Fleming later shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin, the first antibiotic.
But where did that mould come from?
This kind of mould floats in the air.
It is found in every sampled region of the Earth.
You see, it's like smelling toast from a kitchen you can't see.
In 1966, the mould's source was found.
It came from La Touche's room, directly below Fleming's.
La Touche was the colleague who identified the mould.
It was right under Fleming's feet.

claims.claim: Before leaving for his holiday, Fleming inoculated staphylococci on culture plates and left them on a bench in a corner of his laboratory.
Fleming was not a tidy researcher.

On his return in September 1928, one culture was contaminated with a fungus; the staphylococci around the fungus had been destroyed, while colonies farther away were normal, and Fleming remarked "That's funny".
Fleming grew the mould in a pure culture; the broth contained an antibacterial substance that affected pathogens that cause pneumonia, and on 7 March 1929 he gave it the name penicillin.

Fleming's problem was the difficulty of producing penicillin in large amounts; even with a team of biochemists, chemical purification was futile, and penicillin languished largely forgotten in the 1930s.
In 1936, when Fleming talked of penicillin's medical importance at the Second International Congress of Microbiology in London, no one believed him.
Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for the discovery of penicillin, the first antibiotic substance discovered.
Penicillium chrysogenum is a ubiquitous airborne fungus detected in every sampled region of the Earth.
A colleague, Charles J. La Touche, identified the mould; the source of the fungal contaminant was established in 1966 as coming from La Touche's room, directly below Fleming's.

cast.boy: a 9 year old English boy, messy dark brown hair, a round rosy face, striped blue and white cotton pyjamas, 1920s
